en: The *Account of Kāśyapa’s Origins* composed by the Tang Dynasty Tiantai monk Zhànrán is the most extensive among the biographies;
how could it possibly be recorded in full? Kāśyapa is his clan name, hence he is referred to as "the Master of the Kāśyapa Clan" (*Kāśyapa-shì*).
As for "one who carries the diagram," it is like the *Hétú* (River Diagram) of this land. The *Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings* states:

"In the third year after the Buddha attained enlightenment, he converted the five bhikṣus; in the fourth year, he converted Mahākāśyapa and his three brothers; and in the fifth year, he converted Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra."
“Village” (*grāma*) refers to a place where many people reside; however, it is specifically those who are superior who should be so named.
As for “fearing a superior king,” it means that the subjects and their possessions are not permitted to surpass the king.
Regarding the "three abandonments," this refers to abandoning everything from this point downward.
As for the phrase "at a later time the Buddha spoke," etc., the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"The Buddha was at the Kalandaka Grove together with five hundred bhikṣus. At that time, Kāśyapa went before the Buddha while on his alms round and sat to one side."
The Buddha said:

"You are old and advanced in years; your will has declined and your faculties are impaired. You may abandon begging for food and the twelve dhūtas, and you may also accept invitations and receive extra robes."
Kāśyapa said:

"I do not follow the Buddha's teaching; if the Tathāgata does not attain Buddhahood, I shall become a Pratyekabuddha, and as a Pratyekabuddha, I will practice the forest-dwelling life for the remainder of my lifespan according to the Dharma of a Pratyekabuddha."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
It will bring great benefit.

If Kāśyapa were to practice the way of the head (the foremost) while remaining in the world, my Dharma would abide for a long time, increasing the welfare of humans and devas; the three evil realms would be extinguished, and the path of the three vehicles would be established.
In the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*, each of the twelve dhūtas possesses ten kinds of merit; these are explained in detail in the fourteenth fascicle, in the "Chapter on the Twelve Dhūtas."

In the forty-sixth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*, within the section on the eleven items, the practices of sitting under a tree and sitting in the open air are combined into one; thus we know that the characteristics of the Dharma cannot be standardized in every respect.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 49, states that the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) constitutes twelve of the dhūtas; as this belongs to the Shared [Vehicle] and not to the specific Pitakas, the ultimate limit of the teaching is now established in the *Nirvāṇa*.
The details regarding existence and non-existence, as well as identity and difference, are fully explained in the fourth commentary on the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
As for the "four divine samādhis," these refer to the concentrations of the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*); it is through these four bases of power that these four functions arise.
"Formless" means it can cause [things] to vanish;
"immeasurable mind" means knowing the minds of others;
"pure accumulation" means it can transform impurities.
"Non-retrogression" refers to the ability to enter into evil states.

Regarding the "four concentrations," these are the concentrations through which one will certainly attain all dhyānas as well as the outflow-free (anāsrava) states; they are able to skillfully discern and fully perfect the dharmas of the precepts, and by virtue of these matters, one attains non-retrogression.
“King Mandhātṛ” refers to King Mūrdhaja.
Regarding “gods and humans were all equal,” the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
“When Kāśyapa heard that gods and humans called him the Teacher of Buddhas, he rose, struck [the ground] with his foot, and said:”
"The Buddha is my teacher; I am his disciple.
Furthermore, regarding the passage "Again, Kāśyapa," it is as stated in the twentieth fascicle of the *Separate Translation of the Āgamas*:
"The Buddha was at the Karanda [Kalandaka] [Nivāpa]. Kāśyapa and Ānanda entered the city together to beg for alms."
Ānanda said, "The time has not yet arrived; let us go to the bhikṣuṇī vihāra for now.
Kāśyapa did as he was told. When the bhikṣuṇīs saw him approaching from afar, they joyfully prepared their seats. Kāśyapa then preached the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs.
At that time, Sthūlanandā was displeased in her heart and said privately:
"The Elder Kāśyapa preaching the Dharma before Ānanda is like a needle-seller arriving at a master needle-maker's door seeking to sell needles; in the end, they can never be sold."
Kāśyapa was likewise; while he was preaching the Dharma before Ānanda, Kāśyapa heard it from afar with his divine ear and said to Ānanda:
"What is there to find strange in this?"
"Kāśyapa uttered a lion’s roar before the bhikṣuṇīs; rising from his seat, he immediately returned to his quarters.
In the present text, the passage beginning with "Kāśyapa spoke to the bhikṣuṇīs" is the section concerning Kāśyapa’s lion’s roar.
Furthermore, regarding the rules for alms-gathering in the *Separate Translation of the Āgamas*, one proceeds from house to house and stops once the requirements are not met.
Some say that one may go to as many as seven houses and stop if the requirements are still not met.
The "Four Great Disciples" are Kāśyapa, Piṇḍola, Rāhula, and Kuṇḍopadhānīya.
Although the text enumerates seven great [disciples], if one includes the greatness of their original clans and the greatness of the compassion of the deities who yearn for them, they total nine.
If these are taken as the four *siddhāntas*, then "lineage" (*gotra*) and "equanimity" (*upekṣā*) constitute the worldly (*loka*);
the three types of conduct and "greatness" (*mahat*) constitute the personal (*pudgala*), for upon hearing the names and beholding the conduct, all give rise to goodness;
thus, the fourth, "approval by the Buddha" (*buddha-saṃmata*), is the therapeutic (*pratipakṣa*), because through the Buddha's approval, doubts and suspicions are stilled.
The state [of realization] and compassion are the primary meaning, for one enters this state by perceiving the principle.
Both the gathering of the Dharma and the upholding of the Dharma are merits of entering this state.
Regarding the citation of Master Zhao within the section on "Gathering the Dharma," it is intended to clarify that the merit of gathering the Dharma is great.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "of great rank" (*wei-da*) in the text, it does not refer exclusively to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); rather, it signifies that the office held is great because of the loftiness of one's virtue and the weight of one's reputation.
As for the expression "and so forth," although causes and conditions may be numerous, they are all fully subsumed within the four *siddhāntas*.

Next, within the section on the classification of teachings (*yàojiào*), first the objective realm (*shìjìng*) is addressed; subsequently, from the words "Furthermore, regarding... onwards, the distinctions between the teachings are categorized by means of the contemplation of the truths (*dìguān*).
Regarding the objective realm, the phrase "freedom from the five fears" refers to the king, thieves, water, fire, and wicked sons.

Regarding the phrase "the second is clothing" and so forth, one should correlate the numbers with their respective order starting from the first; however, the text omits the practice of sequential begging (pindapāta).
As for the latter three teachings, each takes the first matter as its object, and the expounder must explain this in detail.

One understands that each of the twelve *dhūta* practices gives rise to eighty-eight *anuśaya*s and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; if this is so for the *dhūta* practices, how much more so for other inferior deeds?
Having the honor of being included among those in the stream of the Way, upon hearing this sublime Dharma, would one not examine one's own mental conduct?

Regarding "similar continuity" (*sabhāga-saṃtati*): it arises and ceases moment by moment, yet delusion perceives it as a continuity; ordinary beings, failing to understand this, falsely claim it to be permanent.
All three types of sensation are associated with suffering; even those sensations that are pleasing are in fact suffering.
Movement is not autonomous; because it moves, there is no self.

As for the "Shared Teaching" (Tongjiao), the objective realm refers to what was mentioned previously; however, one should also be able to see that the contemplation of the truths is distinguished here solely by way of its phenomenal aspects.
In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the Dharma-body serves as the basis because one directs the mind toward the Dharma-body while cultivating the two virtues.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth" at the end of the text, it does not provide a detailed explanation of the shaking off [of defilements] across all horizontal and vertical stages, because the various gates of the horizontal and vertical positions within the Separate Teaching cannot be fully set forth here at once.

Since the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) states that "the place of abiding is itself the two," we can verify that this refers to the three virtues (san-de) inherent in the fundamental nature; the same applies to those attained through cultivation.
Regarding the phrase "one is all" and so forth, it does not transcend the three virtues:
"one is all practices" refers to the robe.
"All is one wisdom" refers to food;
"neither one nor all bodies" refers to the dwelling place.
The phrase "and so forth" indicates that the specific characteristics have not yet been clarified, and for now, it is addressed in relation to the dhūta (ascetic) practices.

Regarding the statement in the *Benji* (Prolegomena) that one "abandons attachment to the Dharma" (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), since it says this is attained in common with the Tathāgata, it refers to abandoning both true and semblance attachments.

Furthermore, wherever one may be situated, one leaves behind attachment at each respective stage (*bhūmi*). Thus, the treatise discusses the three virtues (*triguṇa*) of the long-standing fundamental ground, while the provisional traces manifest the robes and other items within the ascetic practices (*dhūta*) of the five flavors.
Regarding the general principles of explaining the provisional and the real (honji-suijaku), these have been distinguished as previously set forth in the section on enumeration.
As for the phrase "and so forth" following the term "contemplation" (kan), there is likewise no leisure to provide a full account of the sequence of the various contemplations.
The "Perfect Dhūta" corresponds precisely to the three virtues of non-arising and non-birth;
thus, the three subsequent types of persons are further correlated with these three virtues, their underlying principle being identical.
“Kṣetra” should be called *kṣetra-ma*; this means “field,” referring to the sovereign territory of a single Buddha.
It is now termed a “banner-pole” (*kṣayastambha*) because it marks the boundaries of that field; thus, many sūtras frequently refer to them as “marking banners” (*kṣaya*).
If one wishes to clarify the four *siddhāntas*, the first is the *loka-siddhānta*, because clans and dwelling places differ;
"Vipaśyin" and those following refer to the *pudgala-siddhānta*, as they collectively establish the pillar of the *kṣetra* to serve as a virtuous cause;
"The Buddha acts" and those following refer to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*, for upon seeing the Buddha, one is able to eliminate evil.
"The Buddha then spoke," and so forth, refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), for it enables one to perceive the reality within the Hīnayāna.

Regarding "the Buddha performed ten supernatural transformations" (*ṛddhiprātihārya*), although ten matters are enumerated here for the time being, the texts of the *Vinaya* and the *Śāstra* do not restrict themselves solely to these ten.

Furthermore, although these matters are listed in the text, they are not fully detailed; the *Ekottarika-āgama* and the *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* explain them extensively. I shall now extract them briefly so that the text may be clearly visible.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:

"When the Buddha entered the cave of Kāśyapa, a venomous dragon emitted fire and other calamities. The Buddha subdued the venomous dragon and placed it within his almsbowl, then proceeded to where Kāśyapa was."
Kāśyapa invited him to stay and provided offerings for three months.
When the time came for the meal, Kāśyapa invited him to eat, but the Buddha said,
"Go on ahead."
He then went to the Jambu tree and took a Jambu fruit.
He continued, saying:
"Though the śramaṇa possesses supernatural powers, they are not equal to the truth of my Way."
Next, he went to Pūrvavideha and took *bīlika* fruits;
next, he went to Aparagoyānī and took *harītaka* fruits;
next, he went to Uttarakuru and took naturally grown non-glutinous rice—all as previously described regarding the śramaṇas and others.
Furthermore, in Jambudvīpa, he took a harītakī fruit.
Desiring to perform a great sacrifice, his five hundred disciples were unable to lift the axe as they attempted to split firewood. Kāśyapa asked the Buddha about this, and the Buddha said:
"Do you wish for it to come down?"
The axe fell immediately;
once it had fallen, it would not lift again as before.
When he wished to light a fire, the fire would not ignite.
He wished to extinguish the fire, but it would not go out as before.
Kāśyapa thought to himself, "I intend to perform a great sacrifice; surely kings and nobles will come. Gautama is handsome, and if people see him, they will cause me to lose my reputation.
If he does not come tomorrow, it will be a great blessing for me."
The Buddha, having understood this, went north to fetch non-glutinous rice, to Goyani to fetch milk, and to Lake Anavatapta to eat.
At dusk he returned to the stone cave. Kāśyapa asked:
"Why did you not come yesterday?"
The Buddha said:
"I know your mind; I have not come.
He then explained the previous events in detail.
Furthermore, when the Four Heavenly Kings came to listen to the Dharma, there was light in the night; the next day they questioned the Buddha about it, and the Buddha explained it to them in detail.
It was the same when Śakra and Brahmā came.
Kāśyapa asked:
"Can you cause my grandfather to come and listen to the Dharma?
The Buddha then caused him to come, and so forth.

The waters of the Ganges suddenly rose; fearing that the Buddha might be swept away by the current, Kāśyapa sent his disciples to investigate. They found that the water did not even reach his ankles, and he was walking upon it as before.
The Buddha said:
"You are like a blind man whose eyes cannot perceive such a divine transformation; yet you still insist that your path is the true one.
The Buddha continued:
"Are you able to walk upon the water?
Now we shall walk upon the water together, and so forth.
If you do not abandon your false views, I will cause you to suffer for long kalpas."
Having heard this, he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet to seek repentance, and then addressed his disciples, saying:
"One should act in accordance with what is appropriate; my teacher is the World-Honored One.
He further spoke to his disciples, saying:
When I saw the Dragon Tamer, my heart had already turned toward the Buddha.

Even my five hundred disciples heard the call "Come, O Bhikṣu," whereby they attained the fruit of *śrāmaṇya*; they then cast all their magical implements into the water, and they drifted downstream with the current.
The two younger brothers had five hundred disciples; seeing the fire implements [and so forth], as described at length, they all likewise responded with "Welcome" and became śramaṇas.
When the Buddha was about to go to Kapilavastu, [the disciples] asked the Buddha:
"Why did he go there? The Buddha said, "All Buddhas possess five common activities:

first, turning the wheel of Dharma; second, preaching the Dharma for their fathers; third, preaching the Dharma for their mothers; fourth, guiding ordinary beings to establish themselves in the bodhisattva practice; and fifth, bestowing predictions of enlightenment upon bodhisattvas."
"For this reason, he went there to preach the Dharma for his father.
Consequently, the King, his father, caused a thousand Śākyas to leave the household life, surrounding him with them.

Regarding the classification by teaching (*yǎojiào*), one should likewise fully enumerate the four teachings to explain the virtues of the practices of these three types of people; however, the five flavors (*wèimì*) are listed because "flavor" subsumes the teachings.

Regarding the correspondence between the three persons and the three virtues within the framework of the provisional and the real (honji-suijaku): a person of perfect virtue must necessarily possess all three virtues; however, each individual is designated by the name of one specific virtue based on what they predominantly represent. This is because they collectively manifest the same essence and share a single identity.

It is the same regarding the contemplation: first one attains the Middle Way, next one negates the extremes and inversions, and finally one illuminates the truths of the extremes; thus we know that the three virtues are themselves the inconceivable, perfect non-arising.

The commentary by Śāriputra cites the *Jātaka-sūtra* and other texts, which likewise possess the four *siddhārtha*. The first is the *loka-siddhārtha*, as it clarifies [the Buddha's] previous lives and his time in the womb;
the section beginning with "Nanda" is the *anuśaṃsā-siddhārtha*, as it causes people of the land to develop faith and see that Aśvajit can produce wholesome roots;
the section beginning with "Devadatta" is the *pratipakṣa-siddhārtha*, as it serves to remedy Devadatta and those who have fallen away.
The first meaning below "In the Madhyama Āgama" praises [the Buddha] for being equal to the Buddha.
Regarding the passage beginning with "In the past," that sūtra consists of five fascicles; this is extracted from the first fascicle, now further abbreviated so that the text may be easily seen.
That Śākya adherent, clinging to the notion of "mine," said:
"In the past, during countless kalpas, my nephew and I were both state-employed weavers. Seeing fine goods within the treasury, greed arose in us, and we immediately consulted together, saying:
'We have labored hard at our weaving and fully know the quality of the items in the treasury; why should we not take them together for use to relieve our poverty?'"
Later, another person stole it from between the gaps and obtained a vast amount of wealth.
The supervisor discovered this and reported it to the king according to the written account.
At a later time, [the thief] came again, and the nephew said to his uncle:

Fearing that my uncle, being weak in years, might be captured by the guards, I ordered him to retreat through a tunnel in the ground; had others seen us, my own strength and vigor would have been sufficient to rescue my uncle.
Just as the nephew had said, knowing he could not escape and fearing that a man of intelligence might recognize him, he suddenly severed his own head, leaving his body behind, and departed.
The King ordered the corpse to be discarded according to the instructions.

The King then ordered a secret watch; however, the watch was not vigilant, and the nephew consequently instructed a young boy to perform a noisy fire-dance, throwing himself into the flames. The watchers did not perceive this, just as the instructions had stated.
The king again brought forth his daughter, adorned with pearls and jewels, and placed her in a dwelling by the side of a great body of water like a marsh.
The king had previously instructed the girl regarding the marsh; she grasped the hem of his garment, and he asked:
"Why do you grasp my garment?"
"Take my hand.
The nephew, being crafty and wicked, had previously prepared a corpse according to the list.
The King said:
"Since such expedients are peerless, what can be done?
When the woman has been pregnant for ten months and gives birth to a handsome son, have a wet nurse carry him throughout the kingdom, commanding all who hear a sound to seize him."
Throughout the entire day, he did not obtain [the child].
The nephew was working as a cake-maker, staying beneath the oven; when the young child cried, the cake-maker gave him a cake, and the child made a sound.
The nurse informed the King.
The king asked,
"Why did you not bind him and bring him here?
The nurse replied:
When the child was hungry, the baker gave him a cake, unaware that he was a thief.
The King again ordered those close to the child to seize him.
The nephew then purchased strong wine and invited the wet nurse and the guards to drink; the guards became heavily intoxicated, whereupon he stole the child and departed, as described in detail.

There were two hundred and fifty horsemen each at the front and rear, while his nephew remained in the center without dismounting. The King then went into the midst of the cavalry and seized him, asking:
"Are you the one who previously committed the robbery?"
"Why did you not seize me when I was before and behind you?
He bowed his head in reply and said,
"I beg for this remaining life."
The King said:
"Your intelligence and wit are peerless in the world; I shall grant you your wishes according to your petition.
As for the phrase "to possess both is inauspicious," when one takes the Dao as the standard, all characteristics that belong to oneself are entirely inauspicious.
Regarding the passage "He served the brahmin Śāraṇa," the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, though seeking the Way for two years without success, then questioned their teacher."
The Master said:
"I have sought the Way for many years without success; is it that there is no Way?

Later, when the Master was ill, Śāriputra was at his head and Maudgalyāyana was at his feet. As his life was coming to an end, he smiled. When the two asked about the meaning of his smile, [the Master] replied as recorded in the commentary.
The two of them took dictation as if composing a commentary (*śāstra*); because of this, they made a vow that if they were to attain the Ambrosia (*amṛta*), they would certainly taste it together.
Regarding the passage in the second fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*, from "Is it possible to exhaust... onwards, the *Saptasāra-sūtra* states:

"Śāriputra saw Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra. As detailed in the commentary on the second chapter, the "Chapter on the Seven Dharmas" (*Saptadharma-varga*), the circumstances of the encounter are extensively described therein.
Regarding the term "the rains retreat in one’s place of birth" (*jāti-sthāna-varṣā*), the Sūtra refers to it as the "place of birth," which is one's original birthplace.
The monks from the place of birth addressed the Buddha, speaking of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra and others, as detailed in the commentary.
"White and radiant" (báizhì): the pronunciation "xī" means brilliant and pleasing.
If pronounced "xī," it means beautiful complexion.
Both meanings are applicable.

Regarding "purity of precepts" (*śīla-viśuddhi*) and so forth, according to the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā*, it is said: purity of precepts consists of right speech, [right] action, and [right] livelihood; purity of mind consists of right effort, mindfulness, and concentration; purity of view consists of right view and right thought; and purity through the severance of doubt refers to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Knowledge of what is not the path as impure is also called purification through discernment; knowledge and vision of the path as the track is also called purification through practice; these two constitute the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Knowledge of the path as the abandonment of defilements is also called purification through nirvāṇa; this is the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).

When reaching the stage of the *yōkyō* (abbreviated teaching), the distinctions between the teachings are clearly demarcated; for the latter two [teachings], one must employ the "identical substance" (*dōtai*) perspectives regarding both *janshi* (afflictions) and *shishi* (wisdom). Here, the statement "the *uyū* (with-remainder) is called *muyū* (without-remainder)" means that from the seven purities—beginning with the purity of conduct (*jikai*) and ending with the purity of knowledge and abandonment (*chidan*)—all are *uyū*; it is only upon the completion of retribution and entry into *nehan* (nirvana) that one realizes *muyū*.

The seven purities are indeed the gateway to the state without remainder; if one were to take these seven purities themselves as being without remainder, then it is clear that what is called "without remainder" is actually designated as such by way of what still has remainder.
Since there is no remainder [of defilements] that can be attained except by relying on the seven purities, it is said that without these seven, there is none.
"Kosala" refers to Śrāvastī. "Vaiśālī" is a place name; its distance in *li* is unknown.

Regarding the phrase "uttering the lion's roar," in the *Śāriputra-siṃhanāda-sūtra* of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, the Buddha spoke a single point of meaning and questioned Śāriputra three times, yet he was unable to answer on all three occasions.
After the Buddha had briefly opened the discourse, he entered his private chamber. Śāriputra gathered the bhikṣus and said to them:

"Had the Buddha not first shown me the starting point of the matter, I would not have been able to answer; yet for seven days and seven nights, I have expounded this Dharma without being able to exhaust it."

Regarding the passage, "The Buddha commanded Maudgalyāyana to go to the Jetavana to summon Śāriputra," and so forth: the Buddha was at Lake Anavatapta together with five hundred bhikṣus; Ānanda attended upon the Buddha as he sat upon a golden lotus flower, the stem of which was made of the seven treasures, while the five hundred others were all assembled there.
At that time, the Dragon King said, "This assembly is incomplete;
Śāriputra is not seen. I pray that the Buddha will dispatch one bhikṣu to summon him.
At that moment, Śāriputra was at the Jetavana mending an old robe made of five patches of various colors.
Śāriputra said:
"You go there first; I shall follow immediately.
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"Is your supernatural power superior to mine?
You must go on ahead.
Maudgalyāyana said:
"If you do not go at once, I shall seize your arm and lead you to that spring.
Śāriputra said, "Maudgalyāyana,
you are merely teasing me."
Śāriputra immediately untied his waistband and placed it on the ground, saying to Maudgalyāyana:
"Can you lift this waistband?
Only then shall you take my arm and lead me away."
At that time, Maudgalyāyana thought:
"Śāriputra is mocking me.
Maudgalyāyana said:
"There must be a purpose behind this; it is not in vain.
He reached out his hand to take the girdle, but he could not move it even a hair's breadth; though he exhausted all his supernatural powers, he still could not move it.
Śāriputra then took the girdle and tied it to a branch of the Jambū tree, causing the entire land of Jambudvīpa to tremble.
Śāriputra said:
“If Maudgalyāyana can even shake the land of Jambudvīpa, how much more so this sash?
We should now fasten it to another part of the world.”
He can even shake all three continents as easily as moving a light garment;
next, he can shake Mount Sumeru, as well as the small chiliocosm, the medium chiliocosm, and the great trichiliocosm.
At that time, heaven and earth shook violently, yet only the Buddha’s seat and Lake Anavatapta remained unmoved.
The Dragon King asked the Buddha:
"For what reason does the earth shake?"
The Buddha answered as recorded in the commentary.
The Dragon King asked:
"Whose supernatural power is superior?"
The Buddha said,
"Śāriputra is superior.
The Dragon King said:
Why did you previously say that Maudgalyāyana is foremost in supernatural powers?
The Buddha said:
"Maudgalyāyana can abide for one kalpa, while Śāriputra can abide for many kalpas."
He said, "The 'limitless concentration' is simply this very concentration.
When Śāriputra entered samādhi, Maudgalyāyana did not know its name.
Śāriputra then had this thought:

"Maudgalyāyana has shaken the great earth, causing countless beings to writhe and die; I have personally heard the Buddha say that the seat of a Tathāgata cannot be moved, so now I shall bind it with this sash."
Maudgalyāyana again raised the question of why [the seat] did not move, saying, "Now you say it is merely that the legs of the Buddha’s seat from another direction are slightly different.
Maudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"Has my supernatural power failed?"
Desiring to go to the Buddha’s presence to inquire about this matter, Maudgalyāyana set out for the World-Honored One’s location; from afar, he saw Śāriputra sitting before the Buddha.
He then thought:
"Among the Buddha's disciples, my supernatural power is foremost; yet now it seems I am not equal to Śāriputra.
I shall go and ask the Buddha:
have I perhaps lost my supernatural power?"
"I set out before you, yet I have arrived after you.
The Buddha said, "Your supernatural power has not declined; it is simply that you do not recognize the realm into which Śāriputra has entered."
Upon hearing this, the Dragon King was filled with great joy.
The bhikṣus discussed it among themselves, saying:
"Among the disciples of the Buddha, Maudgalyāyana was foremost in supernatural powers; now he is not equal to Śāriputra."
He then conceived a disrespectful and contemptuous attitude toward Maudgalyāyana.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Display your supernatural powers."

Maudgalyāyana prostrated before the Buddha and, while still in the presence of the Buddha, traveled to the east across worlds as numerous as the sands of seven Ganges Rivers. There, a Buddha named Citrābha was walking upon the rim of his alms bowl.
When the assembly there saw him, they took him for an insect; [Maudgalyāyana] then showed him to that Buddha.
That Buddha said:

"To the west, across worlds as numerous as the sands of seven Ganges Rivers... and so forth. That Buddha commanded him to manifest his supernatural powers, saying: "Do not allow the bhikṣus to give rise to thoughts of contempt.

He further caused a bowl-bag to hold five hundred [measures] of grain and ascend to the Brahma Heaven; with one foot treading upon the Brahma Heaven and the other foot treading upon Mount Sumeru, he recited verses whose sound filled the Jeta Grove.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they did not know where he was.
They asked the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"He is in that realm," and so forth.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha [of the situation], requesting that Maudgalyāyana be sent back, and so forth.

When that bhikṣu wished to come, the Buddha ordered him to be brought; the Buddha then taught him the Dharma of the six elements to cause him to return, and Maudgalyāyana escorted him back, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "as taught in the *Prajñā[pāramitā]*," that sutra—spoken by Pūrṇa—explains the refutation of views concerning bodhi; therefore, this refers to the universal meaning (*sāmānyārtha*).

Regarding the passage "the various noble ones themselves explain their own dharma" and so forth, this section explains the specific teaching (*pratiniyatārtha*); it cites the *Prajñā[pāramitā]* to show that one must necessarily refute views such as the wheel of the dharma of bodhi while practicing together with bodhisattvas before one can be called a bodhisattva.

Therefore, when citing various Mahāyāna sūtras where bodhisattvas speak of their own realizations, these are all for the sake of benefiting sentient beings or for recounting their understanding to the Buddha; they are not like ordinary people who claim their own views and boast of their own abilities. Thus, it is said that [the latter] "falsely have something to say."

Regarding the phrase "Jizhan" (Auspicious Divination) and so forth in the section on Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana: his father’s name was Jizhan; when he was first born, a physiognomist performed a divination and declared it auspicious, and thus the name was given accordingly.

The five characters "Mugala xi du" are all transliterations of Indic sounds; therefore, in the tenth fascicle of the *Śāstra*, within the explanation of the Tathāgata’s secrecy of speech (*vāg-guhya*), it quotes Maudgalyāyana seeking out a sound, where that Buddha said:
"Mugalaru, why have you come here?"

When Maudgalyāyana replied as stated, it was because that Buddha had called out to Maudgalyāyana using these five characters; this is merely a difference in the lightness or heaviness of the phonemes between the two lands.
In the text, the character "lù" (路) is erroneously written as "lüè" (略), and the character "zǐ" (子) is erroneously written as "xī" (兮).
Regarding the phrase "many share the same name," the *Madhyama Āgama*, fascicle 35, states:
"There was a Maudgalyāyana skilled in calculation who was well-versed in mathematical methods."

In that sutra, the Buddha was staying at the Sārandada Hall in Śrāvastī. After the midday meal, Maudgalyāyana wandered about and went to the Buddha’s location to pay his respects; having withdrawn to sit aside, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to ask a question. The Buddha said:
"Ask whatever you wish."
It continues, saying: "I sustain my life through the art of calculation; having gone forth to join the Buddha's order, I preserve my original secular profession"—this is what it means.
Gomi was well-versed in the characteristics of dharmas.
Because Maudgalyāyana was not uniform [in his conduct], he is separately designated as "Great.

Although the expressions "valued for vision" (*jiàn guì*) and "regarded with gravity for taking" (*qǔ zhòng*) differ in their phrasing, their meaning is one and the same; they both signify that he is esteemed on account of the weight of his virtuous conduct.
Śāriputra was eminent in talent and clear in wisdom; Maudgalyāyana was of noble lineage and possessed a refined spirit—“refined” (shuang) here meaning clear as well.

As for the “arts,” they refer to the Six Arts, which are roughly as described in the *Shiqian*; however, the intellectual arts of the Western Regions differ from those of this land. Because there are those who have attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), that which is encompassed by the four Vedas is extremely extensive.
Within this, the causal conditions also possess the four *siddhāntas*:

the first is the worldly (*loka*), "The Commentary on the Śāstra" [corresponds to] the person-oriented (*puruṣa*); from "Non-Buddhists" downward is the remedial (*pratipakṣa*); and from "Nirvāṇa" downward is the ultimate (*paramārtha*).

Regarding the "disciples on the left side": the reason Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana are designated as the left and right disciples who turn the Wheel of Dharma is that they represent the union of concentration and wisdom—concentration arising from the cause of [wisdom]—and these two dharmas serve as the foundation for all phenomena. They also constitute the pair of merit and wisdom;

furthermore, because Maudgalyāyana frequently manifests supernatural powers, he represents the pair of compassion and wisdom. The principles by which they establish or break the Wheel of Dharma may be understood accordingly.
"Bō'è" (簸峨) means the appearance of tilting or leaning.

There are also variants written as "bō'è" (𧿽𨁟) or "bō'è" (𧿽𨁟), neither of which can be traced to their source. According to the *Wénxuǎn* (Selection of Refined Literature), in the "Fu on the Rivers and Seas":

"Yáng Hóu [the sea-god] *wà'è* as the waves rise along the shore. Since the character *wà* (砐) is pronounced with the *wǔhé* (五合) rhyme, its current form as "bō" (簸) merely conveys the sense of fanning or stirring.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Nanda," the *Ekottarika Āgama*, fascicle 28, states:
"When the Buddha was at the Anāthapiṇḍada Park, Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
'The Tathāgata should perform five tasks while remaining in the world; furthermore, as your mother resides in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, you must go there to preach the Dharma for her.'"
The Buddha accepted [the invitation] by remaining silent, and so forth.
Thereupon [the messenger] departed, and so forth.
The dragon, becoming enraged, released fire and a great wind, such that Jambudvīpa was set ablaze. Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"How can there be such great smoke and fire?
The Buddha answered them fully.
Kāśyapa, Aniruddha, and the others each rose and addressed the Buddha, expressing their desire to subdue this dragon; the Buddha replied to them all:
"This dragon's power is violent and difficult to transform; you may sit down at ease.
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, but the Buddha likewise restrained him.
He asked again:
"How did you subdue him?
He replied, "First, I terrified him with my immense body; next, I pierced and bit him with my minute body; finally, I subdued him with my ordinary body."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent!
You are capable of this."
The Buddha further admonished him, saying:
"Firm your mind and do not let it be distracted; I fear you will be disturbed by them.
Maudgalyāyana prostrated at the Buddha's feet and went to the mountain, where he manifested fourteen heads and circled the mountain fourteen times.
The dragon, seeing this, was terrified and said to his companions:
"Let us now test whether we can subdue him or if he will defeat us.
The two dragons then lashed their tails against the waters of the great ocean, yet they did not reach as far as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Maudgalyāyana tossed his tail into the water; the water reached the Brahma palace and drenched the two nāgas as well.
Realizing they were inferior, the two nāgas became extremely enraged, unleashing thunder, lightning, and crashing bolts while emitting great flames.
Maudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"When dragons fight, they invariably use smoke, fire, and thunderbolts; if I were to do the same, all of Jambudvīpa would be destroyed."
He then transformed himself into a small form, and so forth.
The two dragons, prostrating themselves in submission, thought to themselves:
"Among the four types of birth for dragons, there is no such thing as one who has left the household life; yet this dragon’s majestic power is such that the hair on our bodies stands on end."

The Venerable One, knowing that the dragon’s mind was subdued, restored his ordinary body and walked upon the eyelashes of the dragon's eyes. Thereupon, the two dragons first realized they were not [ordinary] dragons and exclaimed:
"How marvelous!"
"How extraordinary!
he said, addressing Maudgalyāyana:
"Why do you trouble me?"
"What was it that you were cautioned against?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"Yesterday you had this thought:"
"Does this shaven-headed śramaṇa constantly fly over my head?
The nāga replied, "It is so."
Maudgalyāyana said, "Mount Sumeru is the path of the various devas; it is not your dwelling place.
The dragon said:
"I pray you will forgive my transgression; from this day forward, I wish to be your disciple.
Maudgalyāyana said, "Do not take me as your teacher."
"Return to that which I have returned to.
The dragon said,
"I return to the Tathāgata."
Maudgalyāyana took the two nāgas to Śrāvastī.
Maudgalyāyana said, "The World-Honored One is currently preaching the Dharma for an immeasurable multitude; do not manifest your forms."
The dragon said, "So be it.
He then manifested as a handsome man; the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he became a lay follower (upāsaka).
At that time, King Prasenajit came and inquired about the matter of the smoke and fire, and so forth.
The Buddha answered him in detail, and so forth.
When the king saw that the two nāgas did not rise, the two nāgas became enraged and thought further:
"The people of the kingdom harbor no ill will toward me," he said, and so forth.
The two nāgas then manifested a great thunderclap and other portents above King Nimi’s palace; the Venerable One transformed himself into an *utpala* flower.
When the nāgas grew angry and rained down great mountains, he transformed them again into cakes and food.
The dragon became doubly enraged and rained down swords and blades, which then transformed into fine garments;
the dragon grew even more incensed, and they further transformed into the seven treasures.
King Nimi, unaware of this, said:
"In Jambudvīpa, there is no one of such virtue as mine; my palace always possesses such things as these—should I not become a Wheel-Turning King?
The dragon then thought to himself:
"Why is it that my power has diminished to such an extent?"
Having reflected, he finally realized it was the power of Maudgalyāyana; once he saw this, he departed.
The king received the seven-jeweled food and other offerings, but did not dare to accept them himself; he took them to the Buddha and reported the matter to him.
The Buddha ordered that Maudgalyāyana be offered sustenance, so that the king might obtain the power of Maudgalyāyana.
The king asked:
"For what reason is this so?"
The Buddha answered in full detail,
and the king then understood,
as described at length. Regarding the phrase "Devadatta led five hundred [monks]," the *Ekottarika Āgama* (47) states:
When the Buddha was at the Kuru Garden, Devadatta requested to go forth from the household life three times; however, the Buddha did not grant permission twice. Thereupon, he spoke these words:
"This śramaṇa harbors a mind of jealousy; I should now shave my own head and practice the holy life—what need have I for this śramaṇa?"

There was a bhikṣu named Śuddha who practiced the dhūta of begging for alms. Daṭṭhāna went to him, prostrated with his head at his feet, and requested instruction in the rules of decorum; the bhikṣu then gave him such instruction.
Next, following the study of penetration, this bhikṣu instructs as follows:

"One should know the lightness and heaviness of mind, thought, and consciousness; having known them, one should further know the lightness and heaviness of the four great elements. Having known these, one should cultivate the Samādhi of Mastery; next, cultivate the Samādhi of Valor; next, cultivate the Samādhi of Mind and Thought; next, cultivate the Samādhi of Self-Awareness. In this way, before long, one will attain the supernormal powers (ṛddhipāda)."

Through practicing according to these instructions, his fame spread far and wide, reaching as high as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; there, people gathered *utpala* flowers and placed them upon the crown prince’s knees, and so forth, receiving extensive offerings.
Regarding the practice of distributing *śalākā* (voting sticks) in order to break the Saṃgha, the details are as recorded in the first commentary of the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* (or *Zhi guan*).
At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana said to one another:
"Let us go there together and see what kind of discourse they are listening to."
Seeing him, they were filled with joy, thinking that he had come to join them; all the people shared this thought.
He said to Śāriputra:
"Are you able to preach the Dharma for the bhikṣus?"
"I now have back pain," he said,
and lay down with his feet crossed.
After Śāriputra had preached the Dharma for him, Maudgalyāyana led the bhikṣus away, and so forth.
Later, due to committing a heinous crime (ānantarya), and so forth, he was consumed by fire and entered the Avīci Hell.
Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"Where will he be reborn?"
The Buddha replied at length.
Regarding the passage "Saṃyukta Āgama 29" and so forth, that text is very extensive.
Furthermore, the *Ekottara Āgama* 44 also states:
When the Buddha was at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"At what time did the disciples of Vipaśyin Buddha develop flaws and impurities?
The Buddha said:

"At the beginning, it was eighty-four thousand years; at the end, it decreased sequentially through eighty, seventy, sixty, thirty, twenty, down to twelve, corresponding respectively to the seven Buddhas.
Regarding "Śakra’s battle with the asuras," it is fully explained as recorded in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhi guan* (Mo-ho chih-kuan).
"The Buddha’s Brahma-voice is profound and far-reaching," as recorded in the first fascicle of the *Zhi guan*.
"The Buddha sought an attendant," as recorded in the sixth fascicle of the *Zhi guan*.

Regarding the "fourteen transformations" within the provisional teachings, this is fully explained in the *Shiqian*; thus, the fourteen transformations are used to explain the four dhyānas, which all arhats attain.

Next, regarding "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) and so forth, these are possessed only by those who have attained liberation through both [calm abiding and insight], for one who possesses contemplative meditation (*vipaśyanā-dhyāna*) will necessarily attain the meditative attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*).
Next, regarding the "ten totalities" (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*), they are intended solely to cause supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) to become vast and universal.

"Refined cultivation" is as explained in the ninth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* and in the *Dharmadhātu-anupūrvi*, where the ten kinds of "all-encompassing" are presented according to the *Dharmadhātu-anupūrvi*.
"Cultivation of phenomena" is fully detailed in the *Mysterious Text* (*Xuánwén*) and the *Anupūrvi-dhyāna-mukha*.
"The eighteen transformations" are as recorded in the tenth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Mohe zhiguan).
Furthermore, some say that the eighteen transformations refer to "earthquakes" and so forth; now, they are set forth in verse:

Trembling and blazing, spreading and manifesting, transforming and coming and going, contracting and expanding various bodily forms, approaching and entering the same realms, appearing and disappearing at will, subduing others, bestowing eloquence and recollection, granting peace and emitting light.
Furthermore, some say that fire issues from the body and so forth. Regarding the phrase "arising wisdom based on emptiness":

emptiness is the objective realm (*ālambana*). Wisdom arises in dependence upon this realm; since its penetration belongs to the nature of cognition itself, it is said to be "by means of the mind of emptiness-wisdom."

Regarding the phrase "in sequence" and so forth: the functional efficacy of the three truths is collectively termed *abhijñā* (supernormal powers), while from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, it is specifically termed "responsive resonance" (*ganying*). Because the three truths follow a sequential order, it is called "profound entry. Because this is a teaching unique to Bodhisattvas, it is said to "surpass the Two Vehicles"; however, in reality, it transcends both the two teachings and the three vehicles.

Regarding the phrase "not by means of two marks" and so forth: non-duality is the true mark (dharmatā), and seeing the land is spiritual power (abhijñā). Because one sees it in reliance upon principle, it is called "seeing through the mark of non-duality."

Regarding the phrase "and so forth," it is intended to distinguish them: the former two are attained through cultivation, while the latter two are attained through manifestation; the former rely on conventional phenomena (*vastu-dhyāna*), while the latter rely on ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); the former are aids prior to the distinct stages (*bhūmi*), while the latter arise spontaneously in the Perfect stage (*pariniṣpanna*).
The former two are called "manifest transformation" (*nirmāṇa*), while the latter two are called "secret" (*guhya*) and "response" (*anurūpa*);
the former two subdue beings, while the latter two perceive the capacities of beings;
the former two are subject to destruction, while the latter two are indestructible.
The former two belong to the path of instruction (*śāsana-mārga*), while the latter two belong to the path of realization (*adhigama-mārga*);
the former two types of physical supernormal power (*kāyābhijñā*) exist only in the present, whereas the latter two extend across the three periods of time;
the former two are cultivated only upon reaching the stages of an *ārya*, while the latter two are cultivated by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) as well.
The first two [types of aspiration] can be cultivated based on any support, whereas the latter two must have a superior support.
"May I attain supernormal powers" should have appeared in the previous explanation of the causal conditions; however, these four aspirations may also represent the teaching as a whole.

In this text, the first teaching proceeds from phenomena (*dharma*), while the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*) proceeds from truth (*tattva*); since the latter two teachings reside in principle (*li*), they are treated here with ease.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*yathā-prabhṛti*), there are many further conditions that are all obtained through aspiration; yet there are also those obtained by leaving matters to conditions without aspiration, such as the story of Nanda’s arrow picking out the lamp flame.
Regarding the phrase "inducing [the practitioner] to enter the ultimate," etc., the differentiation of the five flavors is as explained previously.
The passage concerning "suddenly having" within the contemplation of the mind refers to the intent of the three contemplations.
The true mark (*dharmatā*) is the middle object; since there is no mind that does not accord with the middle object, it is said to "penetrate and reach" it.
Next, in the explanation of Cāṇakya, regarding the initial causes and conditions that possess the four *siddhāntas*:

first is the world-view (*loka-vyavahāra*); "the *Ekottarika*" serves the purpose of conforming to others (*puruṣa-kāra*); "discussing with non-Buddhists" refers to remedial means (*pratipakṣa*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). This is because the severance of views and the secular classics each involve the refutation of the heterodox and the attainment of the Path.
The term "ornamented" (*maṇḍita*) refers to being skilled in chanting and eulogy.

The term "rope for a fan" (*vījanī-rajjuka*)—if one writes it as "shoulder-carrier" (*skandha-vāhaka*), both are errors—refers to a child whose father has already passed away at birth; because this child prevents the mother from remarrying, he is like a rope tied to a fan. He may also be called "fine-shouldered," because his shoulders and shoulder blades are well-formed.

Regarding the phrase "superiority of reflection" (*cetanā-viśeṣa*): reflection is a mental factor associated with wisdom (*prajñā-saṃprayukta-dharma*); because its power in deliberating upon the meaning [of the Dharma] is strong, it receives the name "superiority of reflection.
As for the ten successive questions and answers cited from the *Dīrgha Āgama*, these borrow the passage concerning the bhikṣuṇī Kāśyapī and the refutation of Pāyāsi to serve as an illustration.

Those who calculate [existence] as being subject to annihilation assume that the spirit perishes after death; therefore, they raise the objection that it does not perish. Those who calculate it as being eternal merely reinforce their own assumption; thus, one must specifically refute them by demonstrating that [the mind] does not abide from moment to moment.

Regarding the phrase "the sun and moon of today" and so forth in the first section, the initial counter-question is as follows: Do the sun and moon of today exist for themselves, or do they exist for others?
If there is another, is it for the sake of gods or humans? It is precisely because of the "other" in the form of gods and humans that there is tomorrow.
If there were no future world, there would be only today; if there were no tomorrow, there would also be no yesterday, for today is itself the tomorrow of yesterday.

Regarding the expression "splitting firewood": when conditions are present, there is fire as if there were a spirit; when conditions cease, there is no fire as if there were no spirit. How could one split a body that lacks a spirit and yet perceive the spirit?
It is as far-fetched as one who, having dismantled the very basis of the conditions for fire, wishes to see it.
As for the phrase "the sound of a conch," the human body is material form (*rūpa*) and is thus visible to the eye; but the spirit (*ātman*) is not material form—how could it be seen?
Just as a conch shell is visible while its sound is invisible, if one seeks that which is invisible within what is visible, one must possess further conditions.

Once those conditions are lacking, even if one turns back to seek it again, there is no principle by which it can ever be obtained; the spirit (*ātman*) is likewise: when the conditions are present in the body, the spirit remains, but when the conditions are lacking, the spirit departs.
By the eighth point, there is no further rational objection to be made; one can only say that [the opponent] has long clung to their position and stubbornly refuses to comply.

Regarding the "two merchants" in the ninth response: these represent the two views of the correct and the false. The ghost is like your teacher; although your teacher is biased, he falsely claims to possess wisdom. Thus, he pretends to be human, using the false to interfere with the correct, and claiming that the false nirvana is peace and bliss; hence it is said that "on the road ahead, rice and grass are abundant."
The old straw is mundane right view;
the new straw is supramundane right view.

The person is the practitioner who rides, and the ox is the wisdom that is ridden. To believe the words of a false teacher and ghost, like you discarding the old, is to lose even the realms of humans and devas, let alone nirvana.

Therefore, it is said that both man and ox are dead, having been devoured by the heterodox; because they have destroyed both worldly and world-transcending [virtues], it is said that "both are devoured.

Next, as for the merchant: he is a person of worldly right view who, upon attaining world-transcending right view, abandons all tainted dharmas of humans and devas. I say, "Right view—why do you not abandon it? When his arguments were exhausted and his stubborn resistance ceased, [he was converted].
Furthermore, regarding "worldly scriptures," the eighth fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"The Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Garden in Śrāvastī together with five hundred people, assembled in the Hall of Universal Meaning."
At that time, the world-renowned Brahmin went to the Śākyas and spoke these words:
"Gentlemen, is there anyone among you who can debate with me?
The Śākyas replied:

Among these two men, one is devoid of wisdom and learning within the assembly of the Perfectly Awakened One; his speech is coarse and clumsy, and he cannot distinguish between what should be pursued and what should be abandoned. If you debate with him, I shall provide you with a thousand taels of pure gold.
The mind of the Worldly Classic thought:
"The people in this land are full of many deceptions; even if one were to achieve victory here, what would be so remarkable about it?
Or, if one were to gain the upper hand, that would merely be a matter of being subdued by a fool."
Having reflected on this matter,
he then said:
"I shall not discuss it."
Having spoken thus, he departed and encountered Paṇḍita on the road.
Śaikṣa thought to himself:
"I shall now go and ask that man about the meaning."
He then went to question him, saying:
"What is your name? Śuka Kātyāyana heard this from afar with his divine ear; he assumed the form of Panta and said to him:
"If you say that I possess only supernormal powers and am unfit for debate, I shall answer your previous argument and further provide a metaphor for you: What is your name?"
The worldly scriptures say: "Brahmā.
Again, he asked:
"Is it a man?
He replied, "It is a man.
Again he asked:
"Is it a human being?
He replied, "It is a human being.
He asked again:
A human being is also a man; how could this not be considered redundant? Yet, there is a difference in meaning between "blind" and "lacking eyes.
A worldly classic asks:
"What is meant by 'blind'?"
Answer:
It is just like not seeing.

One who does not truly know the arising and passing away of beings in this world and the next, nor the nature of wholesome and unwholesome karma, and perceives nothing at all—such a person is called blind.
What is meant by "being without eyes"?
Answer:
It means being without the eye of wisdom as described above.
The secular classics state this as in the commentary.
Furthermore, it is asked:
Are the five aggregates produced with conditions or produced without conditions?
Answer: There is;
it is not without an object.
Again he asked:
What is the condition for the five aggregates?
Answer:
Craving is the condition.
Again he asked:
"What is craving?
He replied:
"This is birth.
He asked again:
"What is birth?"
Answer:
Attachment is like a distant relative.

Having heard the worldly scriptures and attained the fruit [of his practice], he passed away. Panthaka informed the Śākyas, instructing them to prepare firewood for his cremation and to erect a stūpa for him.
Furthermore, in the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the various speculative views of the non-Buddhists are extremely extensive, such as it is said:
"One must not eat while shielding one's form with the hand; nor may one eat between two arms, between two people, between two swords, between two pestles, or between two houses."

Furthermore, it is said: those who first claim to follow the Dharma must not eat; they must not eat from two vessels; they may eat only one meal, swallowing from one to seven mouthfuls, and may accept no more than three additional servings. They may eat once a day, once every two days, or even once every seven days. Their food may consist of rice, vegetables, cow dung, deer dung, tree roots, flowers, fruits, and the like—eating only what falls naturally. They may wear clothing made of grass, bark, wool, skins, or *śāṇa* cloth; they may keep their sideburns and beards. They may practice such disciplines as standing on one foot, remaining in a seated posture, or lying upon thorns, excrement, or gourds. Bathing once every three days, or bathing three times a single night—practices such as these are called "impure dharmas" within my teaching.
Such matters as these should be briefly understood. Recently, there have been those who cling to the practice of sitting alone, yet they have not attained accord with the Great Way.

Those who speak of "exclusive sitting" take the refusal to lie down as their achievement and do not regard the refusal to walk as a virtue. How can it be that while dwelling in a dark room, one’s four modes of deportment remain identical to those of a commoner; yet upon seeing the assembled multitude, one adopts a dignified posture like a sage? Such a person lacks even the conduct of a gentleman and forever fails in the path of a Bodhisattva. Relying solely on their own subjective whims without any standard of instruction, they permit and encourage later generations who lack discernment to follow them, while regarding those who observe proper conduct with the same lightness as blades of grass or mustard seeds.
The Buddha still engaged in the four modes of deportment; how could he have been surpassed by those who had not yet studied?

For the Way resides in the mind and not in external phenomena; it arises from oneself and not from others. Since one cannot contract one's virtues or expose one's flaws, then both manifestation and concealment are equal.

In the exegesis according to the provisional teachings, it is stated everywhere that "one refutes eternalism and annihilationism. Generally speaking, for those who engage in discourse, the refutation of error is primary; therefore, each establishes its own means of refutation within the context of its respective school.
Regarding "relying on the dhāraṇī of the four analytical knowledges" (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*): for now, the samādhi of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) serves as the dhāraṇī.
As for the "four analytical knowledges," they are fully explained in the *Dharmadhātusthāna* (*Fajie Cidi*), where they are applied like medicine to suit the illness.

Regarding "breaking and severing [the views of] annihilation and permanence": this refers to entering the provisional stage of craving and views (*tṛṣṇā-dṛṣṭi*), wherein one first breaks annihilation and permanence.
Furthermore, there are two senses to breaking annihilation and permanence:

first, using various contemplations to collectively break the annihilation and permanence of the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the realm of desire; thus, all four teachings take these delusions of view as their object, as is fully detailed in the tenth fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan*.

Second, regarding the differences in their progressive unfolding and duration: the three teachings all eliminate the delusions of view within the realm of conditioned existence (*dharmadhātu*). However, only the Distinct Teaching first eliminates the [delusions of] permanence and annihilation within the realm of conditioned existence, next eliminates those regarding emptiness and existence, and finally eliminates those regarding emptiness and the provisional; whereas the Perfect Teaching eliminates these three types of permanence and annihilation in a single thought-moment.

Regarding the term "reciprocity" (*wangfu*) mentioned in the *Treatise on the Meaning of Contemplating the Mind*: the intellect investigating the object is "going," and the object eliciting the intellect is "returning. One contemplates repeatedly, elicits [the response] repeatedly, goes repeatedly, and returns repeatedly.
Regarding the explanation of Aniruddha, his lineage and other details are found extensively in such sūtras as the *Bhadrakalpika*.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* also explains this at length, stating that his clan was Kṣatriya.
If one speaks of "Gautama," it is as described below.

If one establishes the four *siddhāntas*, "the Benevolent and Worthy Kalpa" (*bhadrakalpa*) corresponds to the worldly level; "Nanda and Rādhā" corresponds to the human level; "Nandika" corresponds to the therapeutic level; and "the Buddha's Extensive [Teaching]" corresponds to the ultimate level.
The statement "there was no hunting" means that it was avoided because the meat was not obtained through hunting, as will be explained in detail in the subsequent text.

Although the millet rice was humble, because it was the entirety of what was available and the field was superior, it resulted in a superior reward; one could also extensively clarify the characteristics of giving here, but such detail is not urgent in this context.

From the beginning with "Democrat" (Minzhu) down to "Good Thought" (Shansi), including the birth of Yima and the four kings of the iron wheel, there were a total of eighty-four thousand two hundred and ten kings, as detailed in the *Vinaya*.
Regarding the term "grass-initiation" (*caochuang*): "grass" (*cao*) also signifies "beginning.

It is like the first encounter of a commoner with royalty; when it is said, "You shall now don the royal robes," it means one is made to cast off the king's garments and put on the robes of Gautama, thereby causing one to follow the master’s clan name.
In the ancient customs of this region, people all took their teachers' surnames as their own; for example, Zhu Daosheng was originally not surnamed Zhu, but merely served as a disciple of Zhu Fatai.

Since the time of Master Dao’an, it has been mandated that they all share the same surname, "Shi" (釋), as a member of the Śākya clan; this is evident from the text seen in the translation of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
The *Vinaya* states:
"When the four rivers enter the sea, they no longer bear the names of rivers; when those of the four castes leave the household life, they become one with the Śākya clan.
As for the four sons being suspected, it refers to the sons of the junior mother being suspected by the senior mother.
Regarding the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, that sūtra details at length the past circumstances concerning the gift of food and the encounter with the rabbit, as summarized here in this text.
As for the statement "sleep is the nutriment of the eye," it is as recorded in the fourth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Regarding the phrase "The Buddha had eight hundred [monks] make robes for him": while the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, Aniruddha said to Ānanda, "I request the bhikṣus to make three robes for me; my own robe is worn out."
Ānanda went from room to room speaking to the bhikṣus.
He also went to the Sāla Cave and to Kosala; these were different in their Vedic pronunciation (Brahma-svara).
The bhikṣus followed his instructions accordingly.
The Buddha saw Ānanda and asked him,
"What are you doing? Ānanda answered in full detail.
The Buddha said:
"Why did you not entrust this task to me?
The Buddha then spread out the cloth for the bhikṣus and cut it; the bhikṣus sewed it, and it was completed in a single day. Thereupon, he spoke on the *kaṭhina* robe, and so forth.

Regarding the two layers within the provisional teachings (*yàojiào*), the first layer discusses the arousal [of the aspiration for enlightenment] (*fā*), while the second layer discusses cultivation (*xiū*).

When the four teachings are discussed collectively regarding the arousal [of the aspiration], the intent is to clarify that although the completion of cultivation may vary slightly, their general substance is not different. Although the fleshly eye is lost, the divine eye is subsequently restored; thus, in relation to what follows, one speaks of sequence and non-sequence, as detailed in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhǐguān Fǔxíng Chāo* (Commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*).
One should also clarify the exposition of the "manifesting" [eye] and so forth; herein, while primarily clarifying the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), it incidentally clarifies the four eyes.
That the "wisdom eye" (*prajñācakṣus*) is not mentioned in the *Guānxīn* (Contemplating the Mind) is an omission.
One should say: "The concentrated mind that contemplates causes and conditions is the divine eye;

the empty mind is the wisdom eye. In the explanation of Kapphiṇa, the section beginning with "This bhikṣu" refers to the world; the section beginning with "In the middle of the night" refers to the person; the section beginning with "Suddenly" refers to the remedy; and the section beginning with "Vastly" refers to the ultimate truth.
Regarding the phrase "praying to the stars" and so forth, the *Erya* states:
"The Celestial Chariot is the *Fang* [Palace].
The commentary says:
"The dragon is the celestial horse; therefore, the four stars of the lunar mansion Fang (Heng) are called the Celestial Chariot (Tiensi).
This refers to the fourth of the seven lunar mansions of the eastern quarter.
If one follows the system of the western mansions, the correspondence is not fixed, as detailed in the tenth fascicle of the *Zhi guan* (Commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*).

In the teachings of the provisional (yuejiao), the term "qī" (to dwell) is used to explain "sù" (abode) by relying on the place realized by the Tathāgata; thus, it clarifies that the respective scopes of the Buddhas differ according to each teaching.
Regarding the explanation of "Gavāmpati," the initial passage is not divided because it encompasses the four *siddhāntas* (purposes), which will be concluded later.

As for the phrase "translated as 'ox-chewing'": in a past life, he was once a bhikṣu who, having passed through another's millet field, plucked some ears to check whether they were ripe or unripe; consequently, in the final five hundred years [of the Dharma], he became an ox to repay that debt, and even now, having attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), he still possesses these residual habits (*vāsanā*).
The names of the four *siddhāntas* are joined in the middle [of the text] as a general explanation of the preceding and following passages.
Therefore, from the words "Furthermore it says" (*yù yún*) onwards, the meaning of the aforementioned four *siddhāntas* is explained again.
Following the section on "The Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa," there is a further separate explanation of the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the "Verses Spoken by Water," the *Śāstra* states:

"Kauṇḍinya bows his head in homage to the Great Virtuous Saṅgha, the supreme among the wondrous assembly; hearing that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, I shall follow him, just as when a great elephant departs, the elephant calf follows."

Regarding the inclusion of the term "manifestation" (shì) throughout the section on the provisional teachings (*kyōkyō*): if it is taken in the sense of "bestowing a manifestation," it encompasses both the fundamental and the derivative; if it is taken in the sense of "teaching and manifesting," it precisely corresponds to the provisional teachings.
Within the contemplation of the mind, one specifically employs the "bull-king" (vṛṣabha-rāja), yet this also generally includes the "white ox" that draws the carriage.

In the explanation of the causal conditions for "Revata," the initial section concerns the world; the section from "provisional conjunction" onward concerns persons as a remedy; and the section from "the one more" onward concerns the ultimate meaning.

Therefore, if we briefly consider the single occasion of the dispute over a corpse, it possesses only two of the four *siddhāntas*. However, if one relies on the occasion of the dispute over the corpse itself, all four are complete: "provisional harmony" constitutes the *loka-siddhānta*; "ease of deliverance" is the *pudgala-siddhānta*; "questioning people" is the *prātipakṣika-siddhānta*; and "hearing the teaching" is the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.
The account of the two ghosts contending over a corpse is recorded in the seventh fascicle of the *Zhi guan* (Mohe zhiguan).
It cites the *Ekottarika Āgama* to provide further corroboration for the primary meaning.
The account of the loss of speech is found in the *Jin zang jing*.
Within the teaching of the *yōkyō* (approximate/combined teachings), the dispute over the corpse is again used as the fundamental basis for its meaning.

Regarding the statement in the *bekkyō* (distinctive teaching) that "it does not belong to oneself" and so forth: generally, there are three intentions in establishing the Buddha-realm (*bukkai*) within the *bekkyō*:

first, taking the rational nature (*rishō*) as the Buddha-realm; second, taking the fruition-stage (*katō*) as the Buddha-realm; and third, taking the stage from the first ground (*shochi*) onward as the Buddha-realm.
The statement that the ten realms are all not one's own refers only to the stage of the first ground when distinguishing the Buddha-realm;
if it referred to the ultimate fruition, one should have said that the nine realms are not one's own.
In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the phrase "neither self nor other" means it is neither true nor conditioned, nor is it a combination or a separation.

Furthermore, "not self" differs from the two preceding [teachings], and "not other" differs from the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*). The former, in terms of teaching, was provisionally based on the conjunction of the false; now, both the fundamental and the manifested traces, as well as the contemplation of the mind, are all based on the constellations, which is merely a matter of expediency.
“Seeing the Buddha as like a star” is the meaning within the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi*.
Regarding the phrase “contemplating the mind” followed by “and so forth,” one should extensively cite the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi* and so forth.
The detailed explanation of the causes for pride regarding "Pilinga" is found in the second fascicle of the *Zhi guan*.
If these are categorized according to the four *siddhāntas*, "five hundred lifetimes" refers to the *loka-siddhānta* (the worldly perspective).
"Repentance" possesses both [levels of] truth; citing the *Ekottarika-āgama* establishes it as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Regarding the phrase "as follows" after "contemplating the mind," both the general and specific aspects of the three contemplations are the ultimate truth, while the delusions to be eliminated are all considered "coarse explanations" (*audārika-vyavahāra*) and so forth.

In the exposition of the causal conditions concerning Bakula: the initial passage concerns the world; the section beginning with "one hundred and sixty years" concerns the arising of goodness; the section beginning with "bodily happiness" concerns the antidote. Therefore, the passage from the *Ekottarika Āgama* stating "the lifespan," and so forth, constitutes the primary meaning.

Regarding "In the past, he gave harītakī": During the time of the past Buddha Vipaśyin, he gave harītakī to a bhikṣu suffering from a headache; from that time onward, he has always been free from illness.

Regarding the statement "adorned by observing one precept or four precepts," although a lay follower (*upāsaka*) receives all five at the time of ordination, the number depends on the extent of their resolve.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"The Buddha said to Upananda:..."
Generally, that which promotes goodness and extinguishes evil may be eaten;
if it promotes evil and extinguishes goodness, it must not be eaten.
The same applies to those who uphold the precepts and those who violate them.
Regarding the phrase "frequently violating" followed by "and so forth," it should be analyzed as follows:
For example, it is said that if one breaks a single precept, one shall fall into hell; if one observes a single precept, one shall be reborn among human beings.

The reason for asking three times whether one can uphold [the precepts] is to cause one to take the Three Refuges; thus, by upholding even a single precept, one receives the name of a "partial" recipient, up to the point of receiving them in their entirety.
In the sixth fascicle of the *Baoen jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness), five types of trade are forbidden for those who observe the Five Precepts:
first, the sale of livestock; second, bows and arrows; third, the sale of intoxicants; fourth, the pressing of oil; and fifth, the use of the five primary dyes.

It is permitted to use flax from regions such as Kaśmīra where there are no insects; however, in the various kingdoms of the shifting sands, dyeing involves much killing of living beings, and in the land of Qin, dyeing blue also results in the death of many insects. Regarding the aforementioned four types [of materials], it is said that they may be obtained provided one does not trade in them.
Within the Tripitaka there is a single fascicle of the *Pañcaśīla-sūtra*, divided into five chapters, which is essential for those who uphold the five precepts.
Regarding the phrase "the stupa still possesses this power," there are two meanings: first, the power of the śarīra (relics); second, the supernatural power of the protector of the stupa.
Regarding "Great Quiescent Concentration" within the context of the Original and the Traces: it is simply the Great Parinirvāṇa.

From the term "Longevity" onwards, the fundamental virtue is established by means of the events of the Trace. The Original dwells in true permanence while the Trace manifests long life; the Original abides in ultimate bliss while the Trace shows freedom from illness; the Original possesses the eight masteries while the Trace resides in a non-premature death; and the Original dwells in perfect purity while the Trace displays leisure and tranquility.

In the exposition of the causal conditions regarding Kolita (俱絺羅), although it was spoken from the perspective of his maternal uncle to establish the virtues of Śāriputra and followed the uncle’s lineage—where "clan" (*jāti*) pertains to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)—"seeing his sister" pertains to the person (*pudgala*); furthermore, from "leaving home" up to "falling into defeat" constitutes the remedial application (*pratipakṣa*), while "immediately bowing his head" and departing belongs to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
In the fifty-eighth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*, there are several exchanges between Śāriputra and Kauṇḍinya.
Initially, Śāriputra asked:
"What is unwholesome?"
"What are the unwholesome roots?
Kūṭadanta replied:
"The body is unwholesome; greed and so forth are the unwholesome roots."
Question:
What is wisdom? Answer:
The Four Truths are these.
Question:
What is consciousness?
It is that which knows form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.
Question:
Upon what does consciousness depend?
Answer:
Based on life-span (*āyus*).
Question:
Upon what does life depend?
Answer:
It has no separate basis.
Just as there is warmth based on life, or as there is a lamp based on oil, there are many such instances.
The explanation of the causal conditions for "Nanda" is very brief; regarding the statement "also called 'Cowherd,'" the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:

"King Bimbisāra invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus for a three-month *varṣā* retreat. He instructed the cowherds to stay nearby and have them deliver milk, curd, ghee, and other provisions every day."

When the three months had finally concluded, the king was deeply ashamed and ordered him to see the Buddha. He then consulted with his peers, saying, "I have heard that the All-Knowing One is the son of King Śuddhodana; having been born in the royal palace, does he perhaps know anything of the business of tending cattle?"

He then entered the Bamboo Grove, sat upright, and questioned the Buddha; the Buddha expounded for him the eleven matters and so forth, as detailed in the second commentary of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Because he resolved his mind to leave the household life and attained the fruit of Arhatship (*aśaikṣa*), he was named "Cattle-tender" (*Gopālaka*) based on his original [occupation].
Regarding the term "Excellent Joy" (*sukha-nandī*): it is named as such from the initial aspiration for the Way; because it is the most excellent among forms of joy, it is called "excellent.
"Delightful Joy" (*abhirati*) is merely another name for this excellent joy.

If one establishes the four *siddhāntas* based on this principle, then "reversing names" corresponds to the worldly (*loka*), the "one hundred thousand explanations" corresponds to the person-oriented (*puruṣa*), the Buddha’s teaching on the matter of tending cattle corresponds to the remedial (*prātipakṣika*), and the attainment of the fruit corresponds to the ultimate (*paramārtha*).

Regarding the term "Abiding in Joy" (*pramuditā-vihāra*) mentioned in the *Provisional Teachings*, it does not actually refer to an abiding characterized by the name "joy. Rather, it refers to the distinct stages (*bhūmi*); since the realization of the Path is identical [to that of the Perfect Teaching], the name of the stage is borrowed to designate the abiding.
