In the explanation of the causal conditions concerning Sundarananda: the section beginning with "The world" refers to the realm of the vessel (bhājana-loka); the section beginning with "The fourth month" refers to the realm of sentient beings (sattva-loka); and the section beginning with "His wife immediately" refers to the application of the remedy (pratipakṣa). As for the phrase "and so forth," the text is abbreviated; however, the meaning is that his attainment of the Way at a later time constitutes the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
Regarding "Mīśāsai" (Mahīśāsaka), that Vinaya was [originally] associated with Upananda; it is explained here by way of their shared name, as both were upright and handsome.
The subsequent passage concerning "hells and heavens" is explained in detail in the second commentary of the *Zhiguan* (Mohe Zhiguan).
Regarding "contemplating the fundamental and the derivative as before," this is as explained previously in the section on Nanda.

Within the explanation of the causes and conditions of "Pūrṇa": from the beginning up to "this person" refers to the provisional world; "of humans" and beyond refers to the human realm; from "the *Ekottarika*" downward refers to the primary meaning (*paramārtha*); and "desiring to return" to the fundamental refers to the antidote.
Regarding the "praise of fulfillment," this is a reiterated citation of the primary meaning.
Within the section on "Subhūti," the initial passage concerns the world, while the portion beginning with "constantly practicing" is for the sake of others.
Emptiness is the supreme practice, which is precisely karma.
Because its retribution in the present life is even more excellent, he is called Śubhavyūha.
"Abiding in non-contention" removes that which is to be countered; "The Buddha in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven" and below refers to the ultimate truth (paramārtha).

Regarding the four phrases listed within the contemplation of the mind, although they apply generally to all forms of contemplation, their meaning is particularly convenient for the practice of cultivating emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

As for the term "Dharmakāya," it is used here merely to accord with the sense of the first principle mentioned previously; it does not necessarily refer to the Dharmakāya alone in this specific context.

Within the exposition on the causes and conditions of "Ānanda," the section beginning with "The World" concerns the realm; that beginning with "The Middle Collection" concerns persons; that beginning with "The Self-Vow" concerns remedial measures; and that beginning with "King Aśoka" concerns the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the term "ancestral altars" (zòngshè), it is explained in detail as found in the fourth commentary on the *Mohe zhiguan*.
Within the context of the "Original and Traced" (běnjì), the "original abiding" (běnzhù) is interpreted by way of the Stage of Joy; here, "stage" (dì) is synonymous with "abiding" (zhù).
Regarding the terms from "resemblance" (sādṛśya) up to "correspondence" (yoga) within the section on contemplation, these may also be understood as referring to names.
The phrase "and so forth" (iti vistaraḥ) fully describes the characteristics of the contemplation.
In the explanation of the causal conditions for "Rāhula," the sections concerning past lives, the present life, and King Śuddhodana’s joy pertain to the world (*loka*) as a whole;
the sections concerning the various ways of breaking through obstacles primarily concern individuals (*pudgala*);
and the sections concerning the specific obstacles to be broken primarily concern their respective remedies (*pratipakṣa*).
The attainment of the Way is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

According to the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra*, Rāhula was born on the night the Buddha attained the Way; since Rāhula remained in the womb for six years, if the Buddha left home at nineteen, he would have attained the Way at twenty-four;
if he attained the Way at thirty, he would have left home at twenty-five.

Differences in views need not be reconciled; even regarding the various explanations for the arising of slander and its cessation, as detailed in that sutra, the matters are too extensive to be fully recounted here. Furthermore, the *Adbhuta-dharma Sūtra* provides an even more thorough and comprehensive account.
Regarding the phrase "the Jewel Woman and others," Gopīla said:
"I have always been in constant attendance upon Yaśodharā, never having left her side.

As for the term "Jewel Woman," she was of celestial lineage and was barren; had the Buddha not renounced the world, she would have become a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin), and thus the gods sent this Jewel Woman to serve as his attendant.
Some say she was a rākṣasī;
just as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, also took a daughter of the asuras as his wife.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 19, states:

“Yaśodharā, when the Bodhisattva went forth from home, she realized she was pregnant; because the Bodhisattva practiced austerities for six years, she carried the child for six years as well, which caused the Śākyas to harbor doubts.”

Because the Buddha was returning to his native land, Rāhula offered a vessel of food consisting of a hundred flavors along with *mṛdvīkā* (joy-pills) to the Buddha. The Buddha transformed five hundred arhats who were no different from himself; as Rāhula delivered the food directly to the Buddha’s presence, the bhikṣus sat with their bowls empty.
Zhang’an said:
“The Jewel Maiden can give birth to a thousand sons.
The *Faxian zhuan* says:
"The Queen gave birth to a mass of raw flesh like a melon; within the melon were a thousand seeds, and from each seed was born a son, thus there were a thousand sons.
This differs slightly from the text in the *Mahā-śāstra*.

Regarding the phrase "the Buddha requested that she be allowed to leave the household life": according to the *Adbhutadharma-sūtra*, the Buddha requested Maudgalyāyana to ask Gopikā [to join the order]. Gopikā refused, whereupon a voice from the sky addressed her, saying:

"In a previous life, when you purchased flowers during the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, you made a vow that whether your husband was handsome or ugly, you would never be separated from him; you renounced all your possessions, leaving behind only your parents."
"Why do you now begrudge your son?
Question:
For what reason does the text not mention Gopī, but speak only of Yaśodharā?
Answer:
"The one who was Gopikā in the past is today Yaśodharā; the one who is Gopikā today is actually a celestial maiden.
Regarding the phrase "Rāhula at the age of a śrāmaṇera," the third fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama* states:

After the Buddha had finished his almsround, he went to the hot springs at Rāhula’s dwelling. Rāhula prepared a seat for him and drew water to wash his feet; the Buddha took the water vessel and poured out most of it, leaving only a small amount of water behind.
He asked Rāhula:
"Do you see?
He replied:
[The interlocutor] saw it. The Buddha said:
"My description of that path being small is likewise so."
Next, he was told to empty the water, and next, to overturn the vessel; each time he answered the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"That path is emptied; that path is overturned."
They all said to Rāhula:
"You must maintain this intention and not engage in frivolous laughter or false speech.
Then they spoke these verses:
"A madman acts impulsively, claiming that his false speech is right; fearing nothing of the afterlife, there is no evil he will not do.
Having spoken this verse, he asked Rāhula:
"It is like a person looking into a mirror, wishing to see their own face—whether it is clean or unclean."

In this way, Rāhula, you should observe your own bodily karma—both pure and impure, wholesome and unwholesome, as well as what has been done and what is yet to be done—and recognize that all such actions will inevitably result in the retribution of good or evil. You should likewise observe each instance of vocal and mental karma in the same manner.
The names of the four great arhats are as previously stated.
The Buddha commanded them, saying:
"Only after my Dharma has completely vanished shall you enter parinirvāṇa."
According to the seventh chapter of the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*, the Buddha prophesied that sixteen arhats would uphold the Buddha-dharma and only attain parinirvāṇa after a future Buddha appears.
In that sutra, each [of the assemblies] lists the names of those residing there, their locations, and the number of the assembly; thus, all the noble ones individually made a vow before the Buddha:
"By means of our supernormal powers, we shall propagate and protect this sutra and shall not enter parinirvāṇa."
Pindola and Rāhula are included among the sixteen [disciples], yet Kāśyapa is not mentioned.

Regarding the statement in the *Benji* (Original and Traces) that there are "eight kinds of hindrances" and so forth, the intended meaning is that while his fundamental dwelling (*ben*) is free from hindrances, he manifests ten hindrances in his traces (*ji*).
"Obstructing nirvāṇa" means that the obstacles of saṃsāra prevent one from entering nirvāṇa; these are the first eight sections mentioned in the preceding text.
"One kind obstructs saṃsāra" means that it obstructs one from reaching saṃsāra; this is the ninth section.
Next, being commanded by the Buddha not to enter *nirvāṇa*, he obstructed the state of *nirupadhiśeṣa*; this is the tenth.

Furthermore, while the meaning of "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) in the preceding eight passages is slightly different: in the first, second, third, and sixth, the six years spent in the womb are called "concealed obstructions" (*āvṛtāvaraṇa*) because they constitute obstacles such as the womb;
the fourth refers to constant obstructions from previous lives, hence it is called a "concealed obstruction."
The fifth is called an "obstruction" because it is hindered by doubt;
the sixth is called an "obstruction" because it is obstructed by the father, as the father does not permit [the marriage]; the remaining cases may be understood by analogy.

Regarding the phrase "Contemplating the mind follows the previous examples," this is detailed in various texts; here it should be stated as follows: "The provisional obstructs Nirvana; the empty obstructs birth-and-death; and the middle obstructs that which is neither birth-and-death nor Nirvana. This extends even to the three delusions, which can obstruct the three contemplations. The delusions that are obstructed include those that are conceivable and those that are inconceivable.
*Fahua Wenzhu Ji*, Fascicle Two, Part One.
